summaryEn: Hoya follows jang, Korea's fermented soybean sauces, from soybeans to meju, from meju in salt water to soy sauce and soybean paste, and learns why every home's jang tastes a little different.
hoyaIntroEn: Soybeans, salt water and lots of waiting. Let's find out how jang is made!
hoyaOutroEn: From soybeans to two sauces in one jar. Next time you taste soybean paste, say doenjang!
learningGoalsEn: Read and recognize 장 (jang, fermented sauce), 콩 (kong, soybean), 메주 (meju), 된장 (doenjang, soybean paste) and 간장 (ganjang, soy sauce).
Follow the main steps of making jang: soybeans become meju, meju goes into salt water, and two sauces come from one jar.
Know that soybean sauces are made across East Asia and that Korean jang-making has its own process.
Know that jang-making is a National Intangible Heritage of Korea (2018) and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2024.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya sniffs the air. "Something smells rich and salty!" It is {kw:jang}, Korea's fermented sauces: soy sauce, soybean paste and red chili paste. Many Korean dishes start with them.
scenes.captionEn: Jang, sauces at the heart of Korean food

art.altEn: Hoya sits by a low table of side dishes, with brown earthenware jars of jang standing nearby.

scenes.narrationEn: Jang starts with soybeans, {kw:kong}. Sauces made from soybeans belong to many kitchens across East Asia. Korea has its own way: grow the beans, make meju, make the jang, separate it, then let it age.

art.altEn: A big basket of pale yellow soybeans sits by the field, and Hoya thinks about what they will become.

scenes.narrationEn: First, the soybeans are boiled until soft, pounded and shaped into lumps. The lumps are left to ferment. Each one is called {kw:meju}.

art.altEn: Grandma shapes boiled, pounded soybeans into lumps of meju beside a basket, and Hoya waves hello.

scenes.narrationEn: Next comes jang-making itself: the meju goes into salt water, {kw:sogeummul}, and slowly ferments.

art.altEn: A woman pours salt water over meju in big earthenware jars in the yard while Hoya watches.

scenes.narrationEn: When it has ripened, the liquid is drawn off and boiled to become soy sauce, {kw:ganjang}. What stays behind becomes soybean paste, {kw:doenjang}. Two sauces from one jar!

art.altEn: Two tables: one with a dish of dark soy sauce and one with brown soybean paste, and Hoya cheers between them.

scenes.narrationEn: Jang mattered in the palace, too. The Joseon royal court kept a storehouse just for jang, {kw:janggo}, and a court lady called Janggo Mama made the jang and looked after it.

art.altEn: Rows of jang jars stand in a palace courtyard, cared for by a court lady in a long skirt, as Hoya looks on.

scenes.narrationEn: Every home's jang tastes a little different, {kw:jangmat}. Families keep old soy sauce and add it to new jang, year after year. To protect the taste, people floated charcoal or red peppers on it and tied a straw rope around the jars.
scenes.captionEn: Every home has its own jang

art.altEn: Earthenware jang jars with a straw rope tied around them sit in a sunny yard, and Hoya wonders how each home's jang tastes.

scenes.narrationEn: Families pass jang-making down, and schools and community groups help too. It became a National Intangible Heritage of Korea in 2018. In 2024, UNESCO inscribed Korea's knowledge, beliefs and practices of jang making.

art.altEn: Grandma and a child make jang together beside the jars in warm light, and Hoya cheers.

facts.claimEn: Jang, fermented sauces like soy sauce, soybean paste and red chili paste, are the basis of the Korean diet.

facts.claimEn: Jang is food made with soybeans. Korea belongs to the soybean-sauce culture area (dujang munhwagwon) of East Asia; Korean jang-making developed its own process, from growing soybeans and making meju to making jang, separating it, and aging and fermenting it, which the Korea Heritage Service describes as distinct from the ways of China and Japan.
facts.claimKo: 장은 콩을 사용하여 만든 식품이다. 두장(豆醬)문화권에 속한 우리나라의 장 담그기는 콩 재배, 메주 만들기, 장 만들기, 장 가르기, 숙성과 발효로 이어지는 과정을 발전시켜 중국이나 일본과 구별되는 독특한 장 제조법을 가지고 있다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 장 담그기 (Jang-making)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "‘장 담그기’는 콩을 사용하여 만든 식품인 장(醬) 그 자체의 효능을 넘어 … 두장(豆醬)문화권에 속한 우리나라에서는 … 콩 재배, 메주 만들기, 장 만들기, 장 가르기, 숙성과 발효 등으로 이어지는 과정을 발전시켜왔다는 점에서 중국이나 일본과 구별되는 독특한 장 제조법을 가지고 있다." (description read through the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaKdcd=17&ccbaAsno=0001370000000&ccbaCtcd=ZZ, as the portal page renders it with JavaScript)

sources.title: 장 담그기
sources.quoteOrLocator: "우리나라의 장 담그기는 콩 재배, 메주 만들기, 장 만들기, 장 가르기, 숙성과 발효 등으로 이어지는 과정을 발전시켜 왔다는 점에서 중국이나 일본과 구별되는 독특한 장 제조법을 가지고 있다."

facts.claimEn: In Korean jang-making, two kinds of jang, doenjang (soybean paste) and ganjang (soy sauce), are made after the meju has fermented.
facts.claimKo: 한국의 장 담그기에서는 메주를 띄우는 과정을 거친 후 된장과 간장 두 가지의 장을 만든다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 장 담그기 (Jang-making)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "메주를 띄우는 과정을 거친 후 된장과 간장 두 가지의 장을 만든다는 점 … 은 한국의 장 담그기가 갖는 특징이자 독창적인 대목이다." (description read through the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaKdcd=17&ccbaAsno=0001370000000&ccbaCtcd=ZZ, as the portal page renders it with JavaScript)

sources.title: 장 담그기
sources.quoteOrLocator: "메주를 띄우는 과정을 거친 후, 된장과 간장 두 가지의 장을 만든다는 점 … 등은 한국의 장 담그기가 갖는 특징이자 독창적인 부분이다."

facts.claimEn: To make meju, soybeans are boiled until soft, pounded and shaped into lumps, which are left to ferment. Jang-making is soaking meju in salt water to ferment it; after it ripens, the liquid drawn off and boiled becomes ganjang and what is left becomes doenjang.
facts.claimKo: 메주는 콩을 무르게 삶아 찧어 덩이로 만들어 띄운다. 장 담그기는 메주를 소금물에 담가 발효시켜 장을 만드는 일이며, 숙성시킨 뒤 액체를 퍼내어 달인 것이 간장이고 그 찌꺼기가 된장이 된다.

sources.title: 장 담그기
sources.quoteOrLocator: 정의: "메주를 소금물에 담가 발효시켜 장을 만드는 일."

sources.title: 장(醬)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 『증보산림경제』 동국장법 설명: "콩을 무르도록 삶다 절구에 넣고 잘 찧어서 손으로 중간 크기의 수박만한 덩이를 만들고" / "메주를 소금물에 담그는 일을 침장(沈醬)이라 한다. … 침장을 하고 40∼50일간 숙성시켜 액체를 퍼내어 달인 것이 간장이고 그 찌꺼기가 된장이 된다." (only the process is used; this entry's views on where soybean sauces began are not used)

facts.claimEn: The Joseon royal court kept a separate storehouse for jang (janggo), and a court lady called Janggo Mama made and looked after the jang herself.
facts.claimKo: 조선시대 왕실에서는 장을 따로 보관하는 장고(醬庫)를 두었으며, ‘장고마마’라 불리는 상궁이 직접 장을 담그고 관리하였다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 장 담그기 (Jang-making)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "조선시대 왕실에서는 장을 따로 보관하는 장고(醬庫)를 두었으며, ‘장고마마’라 불리는 상궁이 직접 장을 담그고 관리하는 등" (description read through the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaKdcd=17&ccbaAsno=0001370000000&ccbaCtcd=ZZ, as the portal page renders it with JavaScript)

facts.claimEn: Jang varies from one household to the next and is believed to carry each family's history; families reuse old seed soy sauce from earlier years over several years (gyeopjang), and some keep aged soy sauce for decades.
facts.claimKo: 장은 집집마다 다르며 각 집안의 역사와 전통을 담고 있다고 여겨진다. 집안에 전해 내려온 오래된 간장(씨간장)을 이용해 수년 동안 겹장을 하며, 수십 년 묵은 간장을 보관하는 집도 있다.

sources.title: Knowledge, beliefs and practices related to jang making in the Republic of Korea
sources.quoteOrLocator: "Jang sauces vary from one household to the next and are believed to embody each family's history and traditions … some families store aged soy sauce for decades"

sources.title: 국가무형유산 장 담그기 (Jang-making)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "집안에 전해 내려온 오래된 간장을 이용해 수년 동안 겹장의 형식을 거친다는 점" (description read through the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaKdcd=17&ccbaAsno=0001370000000&ccbaCtcd=ZZ, as the portal page renders it with JavaScript)

facts.claimEn: To keep the taste good, people chose a lucky day to make jang, floated charcoal or red peppers on it, and hung a straw rope (geumjul) on the jars to keep bad luck away.
facts.claimKo: 맛있는 장을 만들기 위하여 길일을 택하여 장을 담그고, 장에 숯이나 고추를 띄우고, 장독에 금줄을 치는 등 부정을 막았다.

sources.title: 장 담그기
sources.quoteOrLocator: "맛있는 장을 만들기 위하여 길일을 택하여 장을 담그고, 나쁜 기운이 침범하여 장 맛을 버리지 않게 하기 위하여 장에 숯이나 고추를 띄우고, 장독에도 금줄을 치거나 버선본을 거꾸로 붙여 부정을 방지하였다."

facts.claimEn: Jang-making is practised and passed down within families, and community groups, schools and universities also help pass it on; because households all over Korea still make jang, it is designated without any single holder or holding group.
facts.claimKo: 장 담그기는 가정 안에서 행해지고 전승되며, 지역 공동체, 학교와 대학도 전승에 기여한다. 전국의 가정에서 지금도 전승되고 있어 특정 보유자나 보유단체를 인정하지 않는 공동체종목으로 지정되었다.

authorNotes: Shared heritage: soybean sauces are made across East Asia (the Korea Heritage Service places Korea in the soybean-sauce culture area, 두장문화권), so no sentence says jang began in Korea. encykorea E0048233 argues that soybean jang spread from Goguryeo lands to China and Japan; that view is not used, and the entry is cited only for how meju and the two sauces are made. UNESCO name: the element is written as UNESCO writes it, "Knowledge, beliefs and practices related to jang making in the Republic of Korea" (no hyphen in jang making), inscribed 2024 (19.COM); the narration says UNESCO inscribed Korea's knowledge, beliefs and practices of jang making, never that UNESCO inscribed jang or doenjang. The National Intangible Heritage is 장 담그기, designated 27 December 2018 as a community element with no holder. Left out: UNESCO's and the KHS's note that the practice centres on women of the household (narration says families); the Joseon-era book quotes (농가월령가, 산가요록) and their years; the ratio of meju, salt and water; the 40 to 50 days of ripening (encykorea) as numbers; the buseonbon paper sock charm. 장고 (janggo) is also a name of the hourglass drum; here it is glossed as the storehouse, as in the KHS text. The straw rope (geumjul) and charcoal or red peppers follow encykorea E0076963 only.
